#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#36 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Abstract. Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with the more stable Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. This climatology provides a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structure of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for high-resolution tidal corrections for modern altimetry missions like SWOT, specifically addressing residual issues in coastal, shelf, and polar areas that existed in the previous FES2014 model.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hydrodynamic model (T-UGOm) using a tenfold increase in mesh resolution, a composite bathymetry dataset (GEBCO_2020 and regional patches) with a 2-meter depth threshold, regionally calibrated bottom friction and wave drag, atmospheric forcing from ERA5, and a two-iteration data assimilation proce…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean, with specific focus on coastal, shelf, and polar regions; validation performed using altimetry crossovers (Jason-3, AltiKa, Sentinel-3A), tide gauges, 119 current-meter stations, and GRACE gravity field residuals.
Abstract:
Abstract. The FES2022 Global Tide Atlas represents a significant advancement in global tidal modelling, specifically designed to meet the high-resolution tidal correction requirements of modern altimetry missions like the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission, which demand enhanced resolution and accuracy in the coastal seas. Building on the success of its predecessor FES2014, which performed well in most ocean regions but exhibited residuals issues in coastal, shelf, and polar areas, FES2022 introduces a tenfold increase in mesh resolution, prioritizing coastal and shelf regions. To some extent, this resolution aligns with SWOT’s KaRIn instrument capabilities, ensuring compatibility with its high-resolution ocean elevation measurements in shallow water regions. The bathymetry dataset is a composite of GEBCO_2020 and regional patches from other datasets, with a 2-meter depth threshold to better capture shallow coastal dynamics. The underlying hydrodynamic model (T-UGOm) includes both frequency-domain and time-stepping solvers, with the latter providing more accurate schemes for non-linearities in tides. Bottom friction and wave drag parameters were regionally calibrated. The model also incorporates atmospheric forcing from ERA5 to account for the radiational component of tides when relevant. The data assimilation process uses an ensemble Kalman filter with 358 members, generated by perturbing bathymetry, bottom friction, and wave drag. 16 tidal constituents were assimilated, along with 18 additional waves derived from time-stepping simulations. The assimilation was performed in two iterations (the second one resulting in the final FES2022b atlas) to incorporate the FES2022a Loading and Self-Attraction solution, enhancing the consistency between the model and the observations. The validation of FES2022b demonstrates substantial improvements over FES2014b and other state-of-the-art models. In the frequency domain, the Root Sum Square (RSS) errors for tidal elevations were reduced to 7.6 mm at altimetry crossovers in the deep ocean, 11.3 mm on shelves, and 42.3 mm at tide gauges compared to FES2014b. Temporal validation showed a variance reduction in Sea Surface Height (SSH) of -2.26 cm² for Jason-3 and -5.75 cm² for AltiKa when compared to FES2014b, with even greater reductions (-16.6 cm² for AltiKa) when compared to GOT4.10c. In polar regions, FES2022b significantly reduced the Sentinel-3A SSH variance in the Arctic (Baffin Bay, Siberian Shelf) and Antarctic (Ross and Weddell Seas). Coastal zones benefited from more than 40 cm² of variance reduction within 20 km of the shore. Tidal current validation using 119 current-meter stations showed a 56 % improvement compared to FES2014b, with a global RMSD of 2 cm/s for the major axis of tidal ellipses. GRACE gravity field residuals were also reduced, particularly around the Vancouver Island, from 10 cm to 3 cm EWE (Equivalent Water Elevation). Despite these advancements, some local residual errors persist due to bathymetry inaccuracies, shoreline misalignments, and limited high-latitude data coverage. These issues will be addressed in the future FES release. FES2022 is operational for altimetry de-aliasing corrections and available for download on the AVISO+ website, along with the prediction code on the CNES GitHub. Future improvements will focus on integrating latest bathymetry databases, refining shoreline databases, and enhancing high-latitude coverage of data assimilation through dedicated missions. The model’s unprecedented accuracy in coastal and polar regions makes it a recommended replacement for FES2014 in operational and scientific applications.

Authors: Zhetao Tan, Lijing Cheng, C. Coatanoan, Tanguy Szekely, Jérôme Gourrion, Zhankun Wang, James Reagan, Viktor Gouretski
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6750
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of benchmark-based recommendations for automatic quality control (AutoQC) of ocean salinity in-situ observations, given the heterogeneous data quality in historical profile archives.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A benchmark-based approach under the International Quality-controlled Ocean Database (IQuOD) framework to compare suites of salinity AutoQC tests from seven international oceanographic institutions. The suites comprised 30 individual checks evaluated against manually quality-controlled benchmark da…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Historical ocean salinity profile archives and manually (expert) quality-controlled benchmark datasets from seven international oceanographic institutions.
Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean salinity is an Essential Ocean Variable that underpins our understanding of Earth’s climate system and the global hydrological cycle. Reliable and accurate salinity observations are therefore critical, yet historical profile archives contain heterogeneous data quality, and the community lacks benchmark-based recommendations for salinity automatic quality control (AutoQC). Under the International Quality-controlled Ocean Database (IQuOD) framework, we developed a benchmark-based approach to compare suites of salinity AutoQC tests from seven international oceanographic institutions. The suites comprised 30 individual checks and were evaluated based on several manually (expert) quality-controlled benchmark datasets. We assessed ~6,400 QC configurations in receiver operating characteristic (ROC) space and identified three best-practice schemes for distinct user priorities. These comprised a high-detection scheme with a high true-positive rate (HTPR), a conservative scheme with a low false-positive rate (LFPR), and a balanced scheme with a cut-off between HTPR and LFPR. We further examined their spatial and vertical performance and investigated factors underlying their contrasting behaviour, with local climatological range check and the constant-value checks accounted for most between-scheme differences. This result suggests that regional salinity structure, observational sampling density, and threshold design may strongly affect the trade-off between detecting erroneous observations and retaining valid data. Our results provide a transparent framework for salinity AutoQC best-practice recommendations while highlighting where an additional regional and depth-dependent validation remains necessary. The resulting schemes could support generating internally consistent QC flags for the first release of the IQuOD salinity database and, more broadly, could allow varying data centers and producers to select best-practice QC procedures for ocean reconstruction, modeling and operational oceanography, as well as allow the general data users to choose salinity QCed datasets flagged using the HTPR, LFPR, or Compromise schemes based on their research objectives and tolerance for potentially data errors.

The clearest match for Plastic pathways is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most:

- **It is the only item on the slate directly about marine litter.** The rest of the slate is about phytoplankton production (#3, #9), ocean forecast systems (#5), internal waves (#7), turtle telemetry (#12), and other remote-sensing topics — none of which touch debris pathways.
- **It is a methods paper, not just a result.** It provides a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, with the scripts that ran the particle-tracking experiments and the aggregated result files (#4). That is directly reusable infrastructure for modelling how plastic moves and where it ends up on shore.
- **It is validated against field records** from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#4) — a good template for the kind of field-anchored validation a pathways project needs.
- **It is open and current** (#4), and the underlying trajectories and flow fields are available on request, so the team could in principle reproduce or extend the experiments.

One caveat: the project's confirmed state (goals, blockers, milestones) is not visible to me in this conversation, so I cannot tie #4 to a specific open blocker. If the project has a blocker around beaching/stranding modelling or particle-tracking validation, #4 is the item to pull first.
